title: InfoRMIA: Token-Level Membership Inference for LLMs
one_liner: Instead of asking if the model memorized an entire sentence, ask which exact words inside it came from the training data.
lead: Large language models are trained on almost all text available online, so they inevitably memorize chunks of it. When you ask the model a question, it might regurgitate verbatim training data, leaking privacy. The standard way to catch this is membership inference: you run tests to see if the model memorized a given sentence. But this approach treats a whole sentence as one yes-or-no question, losing all the detail about which parts are actually remembered. This paper asks the question at a finer level: which individual tokens (words or word pieces) inside the output came from training, and which are fresh?

problem.h2: Whole sentences hide which parts are memorized
paras: An LLM trained on billions of web pages will memorize some of that text word-for-word. When it answers a question, it might output a sentence that is partially or fully copied from training. This is a privacy leak: if you trained the model on a person's email, and the model outputs that email, you have exposed it.

To check if a model leaks data, researchers use membership inference: they write a test that scores a sentence and says yes (the model memorized this) or no (the model generated this fresh). But a whole sentence is huge. If even one token is memorized and the rest is new, you get a yes. You lose all information about which tokens are the actual leakers. A beginner might run the test and get a membership score, but learn nothing about WHERE the memorized part is or how to fix it.

callout.b: The standard test compresses a sentence into one binary answer.
callout.html: Ask membership inference token by token, so you pinpoint exactly which words came from training.

steps.text: For every token the model outputs, run a membership test on just that token (and the prefix before it).
Run the same prompt on several other models trained on different data, measure what those models output.
Compute a probability: how much more likely is this token under the training model than under the reference models?
Tokens with high probability are probably memorized; low probability are likely fresh.
Connect consecutive high-probability tokens to identify contiguous memorized phrases in the output.

object.h2: The grain of analysis moves down
paras: The paper changes the unit of membership testing from the entire sequence down to individual tokens. Instead of one test per output (a sentence), you run one test per token (one test per word or word piece). A token is a small unit the language model uses internally—typically a word or subword like ing or re. By testing each one separately, you preserve information that the old method threw away.

hidden.h2: Token memorization probability: how likely is this word from training?
hidden.name: token memorization signal
paras: The hidden quantity is a per-token probability: for each token the model outputs, how likely is it that the model learned to generate that token directly from its training data, versus generating it from scratch? This is measured as a ratio—the probability of seeing this token in the target model's output divided by the average probability of seeing it in the reference models' outputs. If the target model gives a token much higher probability than the reference models do, that token is likely copied from training.

The paper estimates this signal by running two sets of models in parallel: the suspect model (the one you want to audit) and a set of clean reference models (trained on different data). For each token position, it computes a log-likelihood ratio—how many times more likely is the target's choice than the reference models' average? High ratio means memorized; low ratio means the token is not distinctive to the suspect model's training.

heat.caption: Darker shows higher memorization probability; glowing cells mark tokens likely from training.

reads.html: Memorization probability is how much more likely the model is to output this word than a clean model would be. A high score means the word is probably copied from training.
The signal is a log-likelihood ratio of the target model's token probability to the geometric mean of reference models' token probabilities, forming a composite hypothesis test of membership.

paras: A language model trained on data learns to assign high probability to common patterns from that data. If the model saw the phrase 'the quick brown fox' thousands of times in training, it will assign high probability to 'fox' when it sees 'the quick brown'. A model trained on different data (without that phrase) will assign lower probability to 'fox' in the same context.

The trick is to compare two models: one trained on the suspect data, one trained on clean data. For each token, you measure the ratio of their probabilities. If the ratio is high (suspect assigns much higher probability), the token is probably from the suspect's training. If the ratio is low (both models agree), the token is probably a common pattern that both learned. By doing this token by token instead of sentence by sentence, you pinpoint exactly which words are stolen.

stages.s: run token through suspect model, read probability
run same token through reference models, read probabilities
compute ratio of suspect probability to reference average
high ratio indicates memorized; low ratio indicates freshly generated

math.equation: Score_token = log( P_target(token|prefix) ) - ( 1/K ) * sum_k log( P_ref_k(token|prefix) )
symbols: probability the suspect model assigns to this token, given the words before it
probability of reference model k to the same token in the same context
the membership signal; high score means memorized

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Prefix: 'the quick brown' at position 4, token is 'fox'.
Suspect model P_target(fox|prefix) = 0.8 (thinks it is likely).
High positive score: this token is likely memorized from the suspect's training.

math.note: A high score means the target model assigns much higher probability than the references, which signals that token was learned from the target's training data, not from general text patterns.

items.b: Reference models must be truly independent.
items.html: If your reference models were trained on overlapping data, they will give high probabilities to the same tokens, washing out the signal. The ratio will be close to one and you will miss memorization.
Tokens like 'the' or 'is' have high probability in all models. Even if the suspect model memorized them, the ratio is close to one and they look generic. Only truly distinctive phrases light up.
The same token has different probabilities depending on what came before it. Testing token 5 in isolation and in context gives different scores. The method must always include the prefix.
Use independent reference models, test each token with its full prefix, aggregate token scores into contiguous memorized phrases, and use the results to target unlearning (retraining to forget).

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small language model from scratch on a dataset containing known phrases (like a repeated sentence or poem). Then train a second model on a dataset without those phrases. For each, run membership inference token by token on a sentence that contains both memorable and freshly generated tokens. Plot a bar chart showing the memorization scores.
demo.closing: The demo must show that memorized tokens consistently score higher than freshly generated tokens, and that the token-level method catches memorization that the whole-sentence method would miss or obscure.
